text:
Local officials use maritime heritage to foster ties with a growing expat community For many foreign residents living in Incheon’s gleaming, master-planned business districts, daily life revolves around glass office towers, international schools and expressways linking them to Seoul.
Last week, a group of foreign residents traded that futuristic skyline for coastal boardwalks and tidal flats, exploring the islands and maritime heritage tucked just minutes from their doorstep.
Thirty-nine international residents of the Incheon Free Economic Zone took part in a field excursion organized by the zone’s authority to deepen their connection to the port city’s coastal geography and local history. Departing from G-Tower in Songdo, the participants spent the day touring Muui Island and Yeongjong Island, two coastal destinations on Korea’s west coast.
The program reflects a broader push by Incheon officials to help foreign professionals, researchers and students put down lasting roots.
Established in 2003 as Korea’s first free economic zone, the Incheon Free Economic Zone (IFEZ) — encompassing Songdo, Yeongjong and Cheongna — has grown into a major hub for global biopharmaceutical firms, international organizations and logistics companies. Yet officials have long noted that retaining global talent requires more than tax incentives and modern infrastructure; it also depends on helping newcomers feel at home in the surrounding community.
Incheon has become one of Korea’s largest hubs for international residents, with 174,824 foreign residents accounting for 5.7 percent of the city's population — the fourth-highest total among all Korean cities and provinces, according to Ministry of the Interior and Safety data released last month.
The itinerary began on Muui Island, where participants walked along an overwater coastal trail and visited Hanagae Beach, taking in sweeping views of the West Sea mudflats and shoreline. From there, the group crossed to Yeongjong Island, riding a 5.6-kilometer round-trip rail bike track along the waterfront at Seaside Park.
The tour also wove in chapters of Incheon’s maritime past, with stops at Yeongjongjin Beach, the historic Taepyeongru pavilion and Gueup Baetteo, a traditional ferry pier area that once served as a vital gateway between the island and the mainland.
"Even while living in Incheon, I didn't know much about its islands or marine attractions and rarely had the chance to experience them firsthand," one participant said. "Exploring the natural scenery and trying different activities helped me discover a new side of the city."
Lim Mi-sun, director of the authority's investment attraction planning division, said the agency plans to continue expanding cultural and regional programs tailored to expatriates' interests to encourage community integration and long-term settlement.
Through the IFEZ Global Center, the authority regularly offers Korean language classes, settlement counseling and cultural workshops for foreign residents across Songdo, Yeongjong and Cheongna.
